meta.title: Who really said "Safety doesn't sell"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Lee Iacocca is the right name, but only at second hand. Mark Dowie's 1977 Mother Jones expose reports it as a habitual saying — with no date attached.
meta.ogDescription: Dowie’s 1977 “Pinto Madness” reports it as something Iacocca “was fond of saying” — no date, no occasion, no transcript.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1924–2019 · American automobile executive — Ford president 1970–78, then Chrysler chairman and CEO
answer.sourceLine: Credibly and widely credited to Iacocca, but only at second hand. The source the line is normally traced to is Mark Dowie’s “Pinto Madness” ↗ (Mother Jones, September/October 1977), which reports it as something Iacocca “was fond of saying” — a habitual remark rather than a dated utterance, with no occasion, minutes or transcript attached. We found no primary record of him saying it, and the “1972” date that Wikiquote ↗ attaches to the quote appears nowhere in the Dowie article Wikiquote cites for it.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: As a habit — “As Lee Iacocca was fond of saying” — not as a dated utterance

source.excerpt: Safety, you will notice, is not there. It is not mentioned in the entire article. As Lee Iacocca was fond of saying, “Safety doesn’t sell.”
trail: The line appears verbatim in Dowie’s article ↗: “As Lee Iacocca was fond of saying, ‘Safety doesn’t sell.’” That is the whole of the documentary basis — a journalist’s report of a habit, in an investigation published seven years after the Pinto went on sale.

Wikiquote’s Lee Iacocca page ↗ lists the quote as “In 1972” and cites Dowie’s article for it. We read the article in full: the only occurrence of 1972 in it concerns an unrelated federal valuation of a human life, and no date is given for the remark. We therefore state no date.

The surrounding facts do check out. Wikipedia’s Ford Pinto article ↗ records that “Ford President Lee Iacocca wanted a 1971 model that weighed under 2,000 lb… and that would be priced at less than US$2,000” and that “the Pinto became known internally as ‘Lee’s car’” — the cost-and-weight ceiling Dowie calls “the limits of 2,000.”

The sentiment was older than Iacocca. Wikipedia’s automotive-safety history ↗ notes that “In 1956, Ford tried unsuccessfully to interest Americans in purchasing safer cars with their Lifeguard safety package” — the first big attempt to sell safety in America, and it failed. Dowie presents the line as something Iacocca repeated, not something he coined.
source.excerptNote: Dowie’s words, not Iacocca’s. The sentence sits in a passage about the Pinto’s written product objectives — size, cost, reliability, appearance — and Dowie’s point is that safety is absent from the list. He offers the quotation as evidence of a standing attitude, and attaches no date, meeting or document to it. Verified against the Internet Archive capture of the article ↗.

source.rightsNote: The four spoken words cannot be traced to any publication of their own. The work that documents them is Dowie’s 1977 Mother Jones article, first published well after 1931 and therefore in copyright in the United States. quotle.info makes no public-domain claim here.

author.name: Lee Iacocca
author.heading: About Lee Iacocca
author.metaLine: 1924–2019 · American automobile executive — Ford Mustang, Ford Pinto, and the Chrysler rescue
author.bio: Lido Anthony “Lee” Iacocca was the most famous car executive of his generation: the man behind the Ford Mustang, the driving force behind the Ford Pinto, president of Ford from December 1970 until Henry Ford II fired him in July 1978, and then for fourteen years the chairman who pulled Chrysler back from collapse. He was also a bestselling author, and the company he was running became, in 1988, the first American automaker to fit a driver-side airbag as standard equipment — which is part of why this particular four-word line has outlived almost everything else he said.

misattribution.heading: What the sources do not support
misattribution.intro: Nobody else is credited with this line, and this page does not take it away from Iacocca. What travels with it that the sources will not carry is the precision — a year, an occasion, and the suggestion that he coined it.

items.why: Wikiquote ↗ dates the quote to 1972 and cites Dowie’s 1977 article ↗ for it. The article gives no date for the remark; its single mention of 1972 is a federal valuation of a human life, in a different part of the piece.

Dowie writes that Iacocca “was fond of saying” it. That is reported habit. No minutes, memo, speech text, deposition or interview containing the words has surfaced in the standard listings ↗, and we found none.

Ford had already tried to sell safety, and failed, before he was running anything: Ford’s 1956 Lifeguard package ↗ “tried unsuccessfully to interest Americans in purchasing safer cars.” Dowie’s phrasing — “was fond of saying” — describes a man quoting an industry article of faith, and no source we read calls him its author.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest version: Iacocca is the name the line belongs to, on the word of one named investigative journalist writing in Mother Jones in 1977 ↗ — and that is all the record will bear. No year, no room, no coinage.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Four words did more damage to Iacocca’s reputation than any car he built. They arrive in “Pinto Madness” ↗ at exactly the moment Dowie is showing the reader a document: the Pinto’s official product objectives, a list that runs through size, weight, initial price, fuel consumption, reliability, serviceability, appearance, comfort, ride and handling — and never once says safety. The quotation is the caption Dowie puts under that absence.
That is why the line stuck where a longer, more defensible statement would not have. It is not an argument you can rebut; it is a priority, stated flatly, that the paperwork appears to confirm.
detailsBody: Dowie’s wider charge was about speed. The Pinto ↗ was built to a ceiling Dowie calls “the limits of 2,000” — under 2,000 pounds, under $2,000 — on a compressed programme, and his article reports an engineer’s account that raising a safety problem meant being told to “read the product objectives and get back to work.” All 1971–76 Pintos were recalled in 1978 ↗ for fuel-tank shielding.

The irony that keeps the quote alive is what came after. Iacocca ran Chrysler ↗ from November 1978 to the end of 1992, and in 1988 Chrysler became ↗ “the first United States automaker to fit a driver-side airbag as standard equipment,” extending it to all its new passenger models the following year. Neither source we read credits that decision to Iacocca personally, and we do not either — but the overlap of dates is why the line gets quoted at him rather than simply quoted.
context.pull: Safety, you will notice, is not there. It is not mentioned in the entire article.

sourcesVerified.claim: Mark Dowie's "Pinto Madness" (Mother Jones, September/October 1977) contains the sentence: "As Lee Iacocca was fond of saying, “Safety doesn’t sell.”", immediately after listing the Pinto product objectives and noting that safety is not among them.

The same article attributes to Iacocca a goal known as "the limits of 2,000" — the Pinto "was not to weigh an ounce over 2,000 pounds and not to cost a cent over $2,000" — and reports an engineer saying that raising a safety problem drew "Read the product objectives and get back to work."
The article contains no date for the "Safety doesn't sell" remark; its only occurrence of "1972" is a National Highway Traffic Safety Administration report valuing a human life at $200,725.

Wikiquote's Lee Iacocca page lists "Safety doesn’t sell." dated "In 1972", citing Mark Dowie's "Pinto Madness" (Mother Jones, September 1977) and a 26 January 1990 New York Times article "Selling Autos by Selling Safety".

Wikipedia's Ford Pinto article states that "Ford President Lee Iacocca wanted a 1971 model that weighed under 2,000 lb (900 kg) and that would be priced at less than US$2,000", that the Pinto "became known internally as 'Lee's car'", and that in 1978 all 1971-76 Pintos were recalled for fuel-tank shielding and reinforcement.
Wikipedia's Automotive safety article states: "In 1956, Ford tried unsuccessfully to interest Americans in purchasing safer cars with their Lifeguard safety package."

Wikipedia records Lido Anthony Iacocca (October 15, 1924 - July 2, 2019) as president of Ford from December 10, 1970 to July 13, 1978, fired that day despite a $2 billion company profit, and at Chrysler from November 2, 1978 to December 31, 1992.

Wikipedia's Airbag article states: "In 1988, Chrysler became the first United States automaker to fit a driver-side airbag as standard equipment, which was offered in six different models," and that the following year it became the first US manufacturer to offer driver-side airbags in all its new passenger models. It does not name Lee Iacocca in connection with either.
Quote Investigator has no article on "safety doesn't sell" — a site search returns "Nothing Found", so there is no QI finding to defer to.
